newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: SINGAPORE DOLLAR FALL SEEN NEUTRAL ON KEY TRADE.
newsitem.headline: SINGAPORE DOLLAR FALL SEEN NEUTRAL ON KEY TRADE.

text.p: The Singapore dollar's slide against the U.S. dollar will bave a neutral impact on electronics manufacturers, economists said on Tuesday.
But its effect on other industries may be more pronounced in the longer-term, particularly if costs of raw material purchases diverge widely against earnings, they said.

"In general, the effect on electronics will be neutral because most of the manufacturers import components in U.S. dollars and export in U.S. dollars," said economist Andy Tan with MMS Standards & Poor.
Electronics accounts for 70 percent of Singapore's non-oil exports.
Tan said those who had fewer U.S. dollar exports against imports in some other currencies could be affected.
"There would then be a short-term adjustment risk," he added.
Economists and monetary officials shrugged off a clear-cut, one-directional impact on trade competitiveness or inflation.
"Against the top five markets, our currency is fairly stable on a trade weighted basis," said Sim Shyh Yang, economist with Keppel Securities.
He said the authorities had revealed a willingness to allow the value of the Singapore dollar to be set by market forces.
An official from the Monetary Authority of Singapore, the de-facto central bank, told reporters on Tuesday the exchange rate was appropriate to what was happening in the market.
The official also said the impact of the Singapore dollar's fall on trade would not be clear-cut as it had moved in different directions against major and regional currencies.
The Singapore dollar has depreciated about five percent against the U.S. unit since the start of the year but gained against others.

In brisk foreign exchange trade early Tuesday following the MAS offical's comments, the Singapore dollar fell at one stage to a 37-month low of 1.5130 against the U.S. dollar before recovering a little.
Sim said the weaker Singapore dollar was "slightly positive" for manufacturers as it woould boost exports in the short term.
"I can't think of any major sectors that will (suffer) huge impact. The fact is that transactions of imports-exports in U.S dollars creates a natural hedge," Sim said.
Singapore's major industries are electronics, petroleum and petrochemicals.
Electronics experts said Singapore's exports and re-exports to Malaysia were transacted in ringgit and U.S. dollars.
The rise in one currency and fall in the other, against the Sing dollar, cancels out the negatives, they said.
On inflation, economists pointed to the possibility of higher costs of imported goods for consumers.
This could be evened out, however, by competitiveness in industries like retailing, where costs were likely to be absorbed rather than passed on to the customer.
The rise in the Singapore dollar against regional currencies might also help offset some consumer prices.
In the near term, foreign exchange dealers and economists said an assault on the Singapore dollar could see it drop further.
"We were initally looking at 1.50. Now we probably have to look at 1.53 and 1.55," a U.S. bank dealer said.
"Dollar/Sing is kind of stalling around 1.51 now. But if that goes, maybe we'll go to 1.53 immediately," he said.
But Keppel's Sim dismissed any psychological fear that Singapore's currency would go down the same way as Malaysia's.
"That won't happen in Singapore because the country itself, the central bank, controls the bulk of money. We still have that safety net there," he said.
"I see a bottom soon. It should come up from 1.5500."
